cells.tense: What you have been tending is bearing fruit right now, and you are standing in it.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you have a hand in and put it in front of someone this week — say plainly what it took, then let it stand.
cells.core:
You have been tending something for a long stretch, and it has come up. Not a hope in a drawer — a real thing other people can use, in a room where things get passed along. What you carry from that growing is the plain knowledge that steady tending works, and that letting a thing go when it is ready is the next step, not the end.

When it is finally standing on its own, the impulse is to keep a hand on it, to adjust this corner or that, to be the one who decides when it is done. Handing it over can feel like losing it. But the growing was for this. Put one piece out there and let the people who receive it decide what it means.
cells.sheetLine: What you tended is ready to be handed over.
cells.verb: tending something carefully until it comes up abundant, then handing it on
cells.place: where a community keeps what it means and passes it forward

cells.tense: You are already living past the harvest, braced for the season after it when nothing is certain yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one piece you keep reworking ahead of the people around you and leave it untouched for a week, then show it as it stands.
cells.core:
There is a version ahead where this is finished and people have agreed it is good. You are living there, and from there you keep hauling today forward — reworking the wording, bracing for how it will land, measuring a response before it happens. The work is real. Now it is held too tight and fed too fast, and the thing you are trying to bring across does not get let out.

Abundance does not need protecting that closely. Care that does not rest does not make the growth more certain; it keeps the thing from meeting anyone. Let one piece sit as it is for a while, then show it that way. The response you get then will be the real one, not the rehearsal.

cells.tense: You are standing back at a door of an old room and it has already closed behind you.
cells.ask: Put one small piece of what you know in front of one person this week — a recipe, a story, a way of doing it — and stay for their response.
cells.core:
There is a door you are not walking through — handing something you hold into the room where people share it. The offering did not go well once, and you have been standing off from that room since. What you do now you do alone and you bring almost none of it out to meet anyone. So the table you set reads as empty, and the taste you cooked carefully is called nothing special. The material has not gone anywhere. Only the showing of it stopped.

What is missing is not the stuff — you have plenty. It is the small step of showing one thing to one person and letting their answer land. Start small, and stay in the room long enough to hear something back.

cells.tense: You are setting more than one table and you talk as if the tables set themselves.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you already do that shapes how others see something, and say out loud that you chose it.
cells.core:
You are already shaping how things get done around you — what gets made, how it is made, what gets passed along. Other people follow because of how steady you are about it. But you call it simply what needed doing, or how it was done before you, as if the work handed itself down. The doing is real; your claim on it is out of sight.

The care shows in hands that keep old forms alive through change. To take it back, pick one thing you already do and say it is yours — the choice, not only the labour. That can feel like standing on your own. It is not taking credit; it is putting your name on work you have quietly been doing.

attempts.check: The kernel only gives the card as abundant growth achieved and the seat as shared meaning and tradition; it never says what this person has tended, where, or with whom, so every cell must locate the capacity and the bend without naming any history behind it. A reader could object that late-summer abundance can be a private harvest, not a shared one, which is why each cell keeps the act inside a visible, ordinary exchange rather than a feeling. The asks survive a wrong read because each is one small physical act available today indoors, and the closing lines that serve the writer rather than the reader — any line admiring how naturally release flows — were cut before this draft was set down.
